text: Why did Indian merchants and industrialists support the Civil Disobedience Movement? Explain. (2022 Board)
modelAnswer: Colonial trade policies favoured British manufactured goods and limited India's ability to protect its own industries with tariffs, hurting Indian business interests. During the Civil Disobedience Movement, the boycott of foreign goods (in the spirit of Swadeshi) reduced foreign competition and expanded the market for Indian-made products, aligning merchants' and industrialists' business interests with the nationalist cause. Organisations like the Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress supported the movement and opposed colonial control over the economy.
keyPoints: Colonial policy limited tariff protection for Indian industry, hurting business interests.
Boycotting foreign goods expanded the market for Indian-made products.
Business organisations (e.g. Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress) actively supported the movement.

text: Examine the significance of pipeline as a means of transportation in the country. (2022 Board)
modelAnswer: Pipelines transport liquids and gases (crude oil, petroleum products, natural gas) over long distances, including across difficult terrain, without needing repeated loading and unloading. They are the most convenient and efficient mode for such cargo since they eliminate trans-shipment losses and delays, need less energy per unit once installed, and can even carry solids in slurry form, reducing pressure on rail and road networks.
keyPoints: Pipelines efficiently move liquids/gases (oil, natural gas) over long distances.
They avoid repeated loading/unloading, cutting trans-shipment losses and delays.
They can even carry solids as slurry, reducing the load on rail/road transport.

text: Why has India adopted a multi-party system? Explain. (2022 Board)
modelAnswer: India's huge social and geographical diversity (of religion, language, caste, and region) means no single party or even two parties could fairly represent every section's interests. A multi-party system lets multiple national and regional parties represent different interests across states and communities, giving India's diversity far more comprehensive political representation than a smaller number of parties could.
keyPoints: India's enormous social diversity cannot be represented by just one or two parties.
Multiple national and regional parties represent different regional/community interests.
This gives more comprehensive representation of India's diversity than a two-party system would.

text: How is demand deposit an essential feature of money? (2022 Board)
modelAnswer: Demand deposits are funds kept in bank accounts that can be withdrawn on demand, and cheques drawn on them are widely accepted as payment for transactions, just like cash, without needing to first convert them into cash. Because they can be used directly to settle payments and are accepted as a medium of exchange, demand deposits share money's essential defining feature.
keyPoints: Demand deposits can be withdrawn/used on demand through cheques.
Cheques on these deposits are accepted directly as payment, like cash.
This makes demand deposits function as a medium of exchange, money's essential feature.

text: Study the given flow chart of the textile industry (raw fibre → spinning → weaving → dyeing and finishing → garment manufacturing) and answer: (5.1) Which is the basic material required for garment manufacturing? (5.2) Give one example of value addition in the textile industry. (2022 Board)
modelAnswer: (5.1) The basic material required for garment manufacturing is fabric/cloth, produced by weaving yarn spun from fibre (cotton, silk, wool or synthetic). (5.2) One example of value addition: converting raw fibre into yarn, then weaving it into cloth, and then dyeing, finishing and stitching it into a garment — each stage adds value to the raw material, raising its market price at every step.
keyPoints: Identify fabric/cloth (woven from spun yarn) as the basic material for garments.
Give one concrete value-addition example, e.g. dyeing/finishing raw cloth or stitching cloth into a garment.
Note that each processing stage (spinning, weaving, dyeing, stitching) raises the material's market value.

text: Differentiate between the formal and informal sources of Credit. (2022 Board)
modelAnswer: Formal sources of credit (banks, cooperative societies) are supervised by the Reserve Bank of India, charge relatively low and regulated interest rates, and offer legal protection to borrowers. Informal sources (moneylenders, traders, relatives, employers) are not supervised by any authority, often charge very high and unregulated interest rates, and offer no protection to borrowers, making them more exploitative in practice.
keyPoints: Formal sources are RBI-supervised; informal sources are not supervised by any authority.
Formal sources charge lower, regulated interest; informal sources often charge very high interest.
Formal sources offer legal protection to borrowers; informal sources typically do not.

text: OR: How does a bank work as a key component of the financial system? Explain. (2022 Board)
modelAnswer: Banks act as intermediaries between people with surplus money (depositors) and those who need money (borrowers). They accept deposits and pay interest to depositors, while lending a major portion of these deposits to borrowers at a higher interest rate, earning the difference as income. In this way, banks mobilise savings across the economy and channel them into productive credit, forming a core part of the financial system.
keyPoints: Banks accept deposits from savers and pay them interest.
Banks lend a large share of these deposits to borrowers at a higher interest rate.
This mobilises savings into productive credit, making banks central to the financial system.

text: 'To strengthen and assert their national identity, it was necessary to preserve folk traditions and create a sense of pride in the past.' Confirm this statement with reference to India. (2022 Board)
modelAnswer: To build nationalist feeling, Indian nationalists revived and highlighted folklore, myths and icons to create a sense of collective belonging and pride in a shared past. For example, images of Bharat Mata (created by Abanindranath Tagore) personified the nation to inspire devotion; folk songs and 'Vande Mataram' were popularised as expressions of national identity; and reinterpreting Indian history to highlight ancient achievements countered the colonial narrative that portrayed Indians as backward, together instilling pride in India's past and strengthening a shared national identity.
keyPoints: Give an example of a revived/created symbol, e.g. Bharat Mata as a personification of the nation.
Mention the use of folk songs/anthems like 'Vande Mataram' to build shared identity.
Note how reinterpreting history to highlight past glories countered the colonial 'backward India' narrative.

text: Explain the role of Election Commission in the registration and recognition of political parties in India. (2022 Board)
modelAnswer: The Election Commission of India registers political parties for the purpose of contesting elections. Based on a party's vote and seat share performance, it recognises parties as national or state parties, which affects their privileges, such as allotment of a permanent election symbol and free time on state-run media. This regulation by an independent body ensures fair and orderly functioning of India's multi-party democracy.
keyPoints: The Election Commission registers parties so they can contest elections.
It recognises parties as national or state parties based on vote/seat share performance.
Recognition brings privileges like a permanent symbol and media time, ensuring fair regulation.

chapter: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe
text: Explain Romanticism as a cultural movement in Europe. (2023 Board)
modelAnswer: Romanticism was a cultural movement that emphasised emotion, intuition and national feeling over reason and science. Romantic artists and poets tried to build a sense of shared collective heritage and national culture through folklore, myths, music and language, believing that a nation's 'true' spirit lay in its popular traditions — this helped foster nationalist feeling across 19th-century Europe.
keyPoints: Romanticism emphasised emotion, intuition and national feeling over pure reason.
It promoted folklore, myths, music and language as expressions of a nation's true spirit.
This cultural revival helped foster nationalist feeling in 19th-century Europe.

chapter: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe
text: OR: Explain Frederic Sorrieu's dream in the context of democratic and social republics in France during 1848. (2023 Board)
modelAnswer: Frederic Sorrieu, a French artist, made a series of prints depicting his vision of a world of 'democratic and social republics' — showing peoples of different nations, each distinct yet united, marching in procession to pay homage at the statue of liberty. It portrayed his utopian dream of a world of free and equal peoples living as democratic republics, with even figures like the Pope and monarchs shown accepting this new order.
keyPoints: Sorrieu envisioned a world of 'democratic and social republics' via a series of prints.
Peoples of different nations were shown marching together in procession toward the statue of liberty.
The prints depicted a utopian dream of free, equal nations living as democratic republics.

text: Mention any two features of Plantation agriculture. (2023 Board)
modelAnswer: (1) It is a single crop grown over a large area (monoculture), such as tea, coffee, rubber or sugarcane. (2) It is both capital- and labour-intensive, combining agriculture with industry, since produce is typically processed and requires a well-developed transport/communication network linking the plantation to the market, as it is often meant for export.
keyPoints: Feature 1: it is a monoculture — a single crop grown over a large area.
Feature 2: it is capital- and labour-intensive, combining agriculture with industry/processing.
Note the reliance on good transport links since produce is usually meant for export.

text: Explain any two provisions that make India a secular state. (2023 Board)
modelAnswer: (1) India has no official state religion; the government does not patronise or promote any single religion over others. (2) The Constitution guarantees all citizens the freedom to profess, practise and propagate the religion of their choice, and the state treats all religions with equal respect, without discrimination on grounds of religion.
keyPoints: Provision 1: India has no official state religion.
Provision 2: the Constitution guarantees freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion.
Note the principle of equal respect for, and non-discrimination between, all religions.

text: Imagine that you are the village Head. Suggest any two activities that you think should be taken up to increase the income of the villagers. (2023 Board)
modelAnswer: (1) Promote non-farm activities, such as small-scale cottage industries or food-processing units in the village, so villagers have income sources beyond agriculture alone. (2) Introduce modern farming techniques (better seeds, irrigation, cooperative marketing societies) so farmers get higher yields and better prices for their produce, raising agricultural incomes too.
keyPoints: Activity 1: promote non-farm income sources like cottage industries or food processing.
Activity 2: improve farming itself through better inputs, irrigation, or cooperative marketing.
Both activities should directly raise villagers' income, not just production.

chapter: Print Culture and the Modern World
text: Explain the implication of print culture on the religious reforms in India during the 19th century. (2023 Board)
modelAnswer: Print let religious ideas and reform arguments circulate widely and be debated among people, rather than being confined to a small elite — newspapers, tracts and translated texts spread the reformist ideas of figures like Raja Rammohan Roy (Brahmo Samaj). It also let religious orthodoxy print conservative responses, creating lively public debates over idolatry, women's education, and widow remarriage — democratising religious knowledge, since ordinary people, not just clergy, could now access and interpret texts themselves.
keyPoints: Print allowed reformist ideas (e.g. Raja Rammohan Roy's) to circulate widely, beyond a small elite.
It also let religious orthodoxy respond, fuelling public debate on issues like widow remarriage.
This democratised access to religious texts, letting ordinary people interpret them directly.

text: How has Information Technology affected Electronic Industry? Explain. (2023 Board)
modelAnswer: Information Technology has transformed the electronics industry by driving demand for and production of computers, telecom equipment, and mobiles; it has led to hubs like Bengaluru (the 'Silicon Valley of India') where electronics and IT industries cluster together. It has also boosted exports of electronic and software-related goods and services, becoming a major source of employment and foreign exchange earnings for India.
keyPoints: IT has driven demand for and production of computers, telecom equipment and mobiles.
It led to IT/electronics hubs like Bengaluru.
It has boosted exports, employment and foreign-exchange earnings for India.

text: 'The question of sustainability of development raises many fundamentally new issues about the nature and process of development.' Explain it with examples. (2023 Board)
modelAnswer: Sustainability raises questions about whether current patterns of resource use can continue without damaging the environment for future generations — e.g. unchecked groundwater extraction for agriculture is depleting water tables in many regions, and unsustainable use of forests and fossil fuels harms ecological balance. This forces planners to reconsider growth models, e.g. promoting rainwater harvesting or renewable energy instead of purely maximising short-term output, showing sustainability changes what 'development' itself should mean.
keyPoints: Give an example of unsustainable resource use, e.g. excessive groundwater extraction.
Note that such practices benefit the present generation while harming future generations' resources.
Explain how this forces new development approaches, e.g. rainwater harvesting or renewable energy.

text: Explain any three functions of Political Party. (2023 Board)
modelAnswer: (1) Contesting elections by selecting and putting up candidates. (2) Forming and running the government if elected, or performing the role of opposition if not, to keep the ruling party in check. (3) Shaping public opinion and mobilising citizens on public issues, and giving them access to government machinery/welfare benefits through local representatives.
keyPoints: Function 1: contesting elections by putting up candidates.
Function 2: forming government or playing the opposition role.
Function 3: shaping public opinion and giving citizens access to government machinery.

text: Explain any three functions of the Reserve Bank of India. (2023 Board)
modelAnswer: (1) The RBI supervises and regulates the functioning of formal-sector banks and financial institutions in the country. (2) It acts as the 'banker's bank' and controls money supply/credit through monetary policy. (3) It issues currency notes (except coins and one-rupee notes) and manages the country's foreign exchange reserves, ensuring monetary stability.
keyPoints: Function 1: supervising/regulating banks and financial institutions.
Function 2: acting as the banker's bank and controlling money supply via monetary policy.
Function 3: issuing currency notes and managing foreign exchange reserves.

text: OR: Explain the role of banks with regard to money which they accept from the public. (2023 Board)
modelAnswer: Banks accept deposits from the public and pay interest on them, keeping only a small portion as a cash reserve for withdrawal demands, while lending out the major share to borrowers at a higher interest rate. This interest-rate difference is the bank's main source of income, and this intermediation between depositors and borrowers is banks' central economic role.
keyPoints: Banks accept public deposits and pay interest, keeping only a small cash reserve.
They lend the larger share of deposits to borrowers at a higher interest rate.
The interest-rate spread is the bank's income, making this intermediation its central role.

chapter: The Making of a Global World
text: 'The Silk route was a good example of vibrant pre-modern trade and cultural links between distant parts of the world.' Explain the statement with any two examples. (2024 Board)
modelAnswer: The Silk Route linked Europe and Asia through trade in Chinese silk, but also carried pottery, textiles and spices across vast distances. (1) Chinese pottery and textiles travelled west along these routes while goods travelled east in turn. (2) Cultural and religious exchange occurred too — Buddhism spread from India to Central Asia and China via these routes, and foods like coffee and cocoa reached Europe through similar exchanges, showing the routes carried culture as much as commerce.
keyPoints: Note the Silk Route carried goods (silk, pottery, textiles, spices) both ways across Asia and Europe.
Give one trade example, e.g. Chinese pottery/textiles moving west.
Give one cultural example, e.g. Buddhism's spread to China, or new foods reaching Europe.

text: Suggest any two measures for the conservation of forest. (2024 Board)
modelAnswer: (1) Community/Joint Forest Management: involving local communities in protecting and managing forests so people have a stake in conservation. (2) Afforestation and strict enforcement of laws against illegal logging and encroachment, along with creating protected areas (reserved/protected forests) to prevent overexploitation.
keyPoints: Measure 1: community-based/joint forest management involving local people.
Measure 2: afforestation plus strict enforcement against illegal logging/encroachment.
Mention protected-area designations (reserved/protected forests) as another safeguard.

text: OR: Suggest any two measures for the conservation of wildlife. (2024 Board)
modelAnswer: (1) Establishing and effectively managing protected areas — national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and biosphere reserves — to give threatened species a safe habitat. (2) Running special conservation projects for endangered species (e.g. Project Tiger, Project Elephant) and strictly enforcing anti-poaching laws to prevent illegal hunting and trade.
keyPoints: Measure 1: protected areas (national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves).
Measure 2: species-specific projects (e.g. Project Tiger) and anti-poaching enforcement.
Both measures should target giving threatened species a safe, monitored habitat.

text: Why is power sharing desirable? Explain. (2024 Board)
modelAnswer: Power sharing is desirable for two broad reasons: a prudential reason — it reduces the possibility of conflict between social groups, since sharing power reduces the risk of one group dominating another and increases political stability; and a moral reason — power sharing is the very spirit of democracy, since a legitimate democratic government must involve as many people/groups as possible in decisions that affect them, rather than concentrating power in a few hands.
keyPoints: Prudential reason: power sharing reduces conflict between social groups and increases stability.
Moral reason: power sharing reflects the basic spirit of democracy — involving people in decisions.
Both reasons should be stated, not just one.

text: Differentiate between Public and Private Sector. (2024 Board)
modelAnswer: The public sector is owned and run by the government (e.g. Railways, BHEL), typically aiming at public welfare besides revenue, often in areas needing large investment or essential services. The private sector is owned and run by private individuals or companies (e.g. TISCO, Reliance), primarily driven by profit, and operates in competitive market conditions across many industries.
keyPoints: Public sector: government-owned, aims at public welfare as well as revenue.
Private sector: privately owned, primarily profit-driven.
Give one example of each (e.g. Railways for public, Reliance for private).

text: Describe any three causes that led to the Non-Cooperation Movement. (2024 Board)
modelAnswer: (1) The Rowlatt Act (1919) curtailed civil liberties and allowed detention without trial, angering Indians. (2) The Jallianwala Bagh massacre (1919), where General Dyer ordered firing on an unarmed peaceful crowd at Amritsar, outraged the nation. (3) Support for the Khilafat cause — Indian Muslims were upset over the treatment of the Ottoman Caliph after WWI, and Gandhi saw an opportunity to unite Hindus and Muslims in a joint movement against colonial rule.
keyPoints: Cause 1: the repressive Rowlatt Act (1919).
Cause 2: the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (1919).
Cause 3: the Khilafat movement, which Gandhi used to unite Hindus and Muslims.

text: OR: Describe any three causes of 'Civil Disobedience Movement.' (2024 Board)
modelAnswer: (1) The Simon Commission (1928) had no Indian members, which was seen as an insult and sparked widespread protest. (2) The Congress's demand for 'Purna Swaraj' (complete independence), declared at the Lahore session (1929), set the stage for a new mass movement. (3) Gandhi's Dandi March/Salt Satyagraha (1930) against the salt tax and government monopoly on salt symbolically challenged British authority and triggered mass civil disobedience.
keyPoints: Cause 1: the all-European Simon Commission (1928), seen as insulting.
Cause 2: the Lahore session's (1929) demand for 'Purna Swaraj'.
Cause 3: the Dandi March/Salt Satyagraha (1930), which symbolically triggered the movement.

text: 'Manufacturing industries are considered the backbone of economic development.' Justify the statement. (2024 Board)
modelAnswer: (1) Manufacturing modernises agriculture by generating demand for and supplying farm inputs like tractors, fertilisers and pesticides, linking industry to the primary sector. (2) It reduces dependence on the export of raw agricultural produce, promoting export of manufactured goods and earning more foreign exchange. (3) It generates large-scale employment, helping to reduce unemployment and poverty, and lets a country fully use its natural and human resources.
keyPoints: Reason 1: manufacturing supplies inputs (tractors, fertilisers) that modernise agriculture.
Reason 2: it shifts exports from raw produce to higher-value manufactured goods.
Reason 3: it generates large-scale employment, reducing unemployment/poverty.

text: Analyse the role of political parties in a democracy. (2024 Board)
modelAnswer: Political parties contest elections, giving voters a choice among candidates and programmes; form and run the government when they win a majority, translating their manifesto into policy; act as the main opposition when they lose, checking the ruling party; shape public opinion through campaigns and debates; and give people access to government machinery and welfare schemes through local representatives. Without parties, modern representative democracy would lack organisation for elections and governance.
keyPoints: Parties contest elections and, if elected, form and run the government.
The losing parties play the opposition role, checking the ruling party.
Parties shape public opinion and connect citizens to government machinery/welfare schemes.

text: How is credit essential for economic activities? Explain with examples. (2024 Board)
modelAnswer: Credit lets people undertake economic activities that need money upfront before returns come in — e.g. a farmer borrows to buy seeds and fertiliser before harvest, or a small business owner borrows working capital to buy raw material before selling finished goods. Timely, affordable credit can grow incomes (e.g. a farmer investing loan money in better inputs may get a much higher harvest, comfortably repaying the loan and still profiting), showing credit's crucial, positive role in economic activity when available on reasonable terms.
keyPoints: Explain that credit provides upfront funds needed before economic returns arrive.
Give a concrete example, e.g. a farmer borrowing for seeds/fertiliser before harvest.
Note that affordable, timely credit can raise incomes, while costly credit can trap borrowers in debt.

text: How is the issue of sustainability important for development? Explain. (2024 Board)
modelAnswer: Development that depletes resources unsustainably — such as excessive groundwater withdrawal or deforestation — may benefit the present generation but leaves future generations with fewer resources and a degraded environment. Sustainable development requires balancing today's needs with conserving resources (renewable energy, judicious water use, resource-efficient practices), so economic growth can continue for future generations too, without irreversible ecological damage.
keyPoints: Give an example of unsustainable resource use, e.g. excessive groundwater withdrawal.
Explain that such use benefits the present generation at the cost of future generations.
Note that sustainable development balances today's needs against resource conservation for the future.

chapter: The Making of a Global World
text: How had globalization begun long before the sixteenth century? Explain. (2025 Board)
modelAnswer: Long before the 16th century, trade, migration and the movement of goods, people and even crops already connected distant parts of the world — for example, the Silk Route carried silk, textiles and precious metals between Asia, Africa and Europe, and crops like wheat and various spices spread across continents through trade and travel. This shows extensive networks of trade and cultural exchange existed well before formal 16th-century European expansion.
keyPoints: Cite pre-modern trade networks, e.g. the Silk Route linking Asia, Africa and Europe.
Note the movement of crops/goods across continents through trade and travel.
Conclude that extensive global connections pre-dated 16th-century European expansion.

chapter: The Making of a Global World
text: OR: How did trade help to spread diseases during the pre-modern world? Explain. (2025 Board)
modelAnswer: Trade routes connected distant populations, and travellers and traders carried diseases along with goods. For example, the plague originated in Asia and spread to Europe via trade routes in the 14th century, killing a significant share of the population. Similarly, European traders and conquerors carried diseases like smallpox to the Americas, devastating indigenous populations who had no immunity to these new pathogens.
keyPoints: Explain that trade routes connected populations, letting diseases travel along with traders.
Give the example of the plague spreading from Asia to Europe in the 14th century.
Give the example of smallpox devastating indigenous American populations after European contact.

chapter: Print Culture and the Modern World
text: Explain the role of Johann Gutenberg in the spread of print culture in Europe. (2025 Board)
modelAnswer: Johann Gutenberg developed the printing press with movable metal type in Germany around the 1430s-40s, adapting existing technologies (like the olive/wine press) to mechanically print books instead of copying them by hand. His first major printed work was the Bible. This innovation let books be produced much faster and more cheaply than manual copying, spreading literacy and print culture rapidly across Europe.
keyPoints: Gutenberg developed the printing press with movable metal type in the 1430s-40s.
He adapted existing mechanical technology (e.g. the olive press) for printing; his first major book was the Bible.
This let books be produced faster and cheaper, spreading literacy and print culture across Europe.

chapter: Print Culture and the Modern World
text: OR: Explain the role of print in the expansion of protestant reformation. (2025 Board)
modelAnswer: Print allowed Martin Luther's Ninety Five Theses (1517), criticising the Catholic Church, to be reproduced and circulated quickly and widely, spreading his ideas far beyond what a hand-copied manuscript could reach. Print also made translated religious texts (like the Bible) accessible to ordinary people, letting them read and interpret scripture themselves rather than relying solely on the clergy — this combination of fast-spreading criticism and accessible scripture fuelled the Reformation's rapid spread across Europe.
keyPoints: Print let Luther's Ninety Five Theses (1517) spread quickly and widely.
It made translated religious texts (e.g. the Bible) accessible to ordinary readers.
This combination of fast-spreading criticism and accessible scripture fuelled the Reformation.

text: Suggest any two measures for better productivity and organic farming. (2025 Board)
modelAnswer: (1) Use high-yielding variety (HYV) seeds along with adequate, timely irrigation and balanced use of fertilisers to raise productivity. (2) Promote organic farming through bio-fertilisers, crop rotation and vermi-composting, reducing chemical fertiliser/pesticide use to maintain soil health and long-term sustainability.
keyPoints: Measure 1: HYV seeds with adequate irrigation and balanced fertiliser use for productivity.
Measure 2: organic practices — bio-fertilisers, crop rotation, vermi-composting.
Note the aim of reducing chemical input use to protect long-term soil health.

text: Explain any two features of federalism. (2025 Board)
modelAnswer: (1) There are two or more levels/tiers of government (e.g. central and state governments in India) governing the same citizens. (2) Each tier has its own distinct jurisdiction/powers as specified in the Constitution, and this jurisdiction is constitutionally guaranteed — one level of government cannot unilaterally alter the powers of another.
keyPoints: Feature 1: two or more levels of government governing the same citizens.
Feature 2: each level has its own constitutionally guaranteed jurisdiction.
Note that no single level can unilaterally change another's powers.

text: Explain any two Constitutional provisions that make India a secular nation. (2025 Board)
modelAnswer: (1) India has no official religion — the state does not promote or patronise any particular religion. (2) The Constitution guarantees all individuals and communities the freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion (Article 25), and prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion.
keyPoints: Provision 1: no official state religion.
Provision 2: freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion (Article 25).
Note the principle of non-discrimination on religious grounds.

text: 'Political parties perform a series of functions in the democracy.' Explain the statement with examples. (2025 Board)
modelAnswer: Political parties: contest elections and put up candidates (e.g. national and regional parties fielding candidates); form and run governments when they win a majority; play the role of opposition when they lose, checking the ruling party's actions; shape public opinion through campaigns and mobilise citizens; and provide people access to government machinery and welfare benefits through their local representatives.
keyPoints: Function: contesting elections by putting up candidates.
Function: forming government or playing the opposition role.
Function: shaping public opinion and connecting citizens to government machinery.

text: 'New technology has helped the world to become connected.' Justify the statement with suitable arguments. (2025 Board)
modelAnswer: Rapid improvements in transport technology (faster ships, aviation) and information technology (telecommunications, computers, the internet) have reduced the time and cost of moving goods, services, capital and information across long distances. This lets businesses fragment production across countries and connect distant markets instantly, which is precisely what has driven the rapid pace of globalisation in recent decades.
keyPoints: Cite faster/cheaper transport technology (ships, aviation) reducing distance's cost.
Cite information technology (telecom, internet) enabling instant communication and coordination.
Link these directly to enabling globalised production and markets.

text: Differentiate between formal and informal sources of credit. (2025 Board)
modelAnswer: Formal sources (banks, cooperative societies) are supervised by the Reserve Bank of India, charge relatively low, regulated interest rates, and offer borrowers legal protection. Informal sources (moneylenders, traders, relatives, employers) are not supervised by any regulatory authority, often charge very high, unregulated interest rates, and offer borrowers no protection against exploitative practices.
keyPoints: Formal sources are RBI-supervised; informal sources are unsupervised.
Formal sources charge lower, regulated interest; informal sources often charge exploitative rates.
Formal sources offer legal protection to borrowers; informal sources typically do not.

text: Why is sustainable development essential? Explain with examples. (2025 Board)
modelAnswer: Sustainable development ensures resources are used in ways that meet present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet their own needs. Examples: judicious use of groundwater through rainwater harvesting, adopting renewable energy (solar/wind) to reduce fossil-fuel depletion, and equitable resource distribution — all preventing resource exhaustion and environmental degradation for future generations.
keyPoints: Define sustainable development as meeting present needs without harming future generations.
Give the example of rainwater harvesting for judicious groundwater use.
Give the example of renewable energy (solar/wind) reducing fossil-fuel depletion.

text: Explain the role of anti-colonial movement in the rise of 'modern nationalism' in India. (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: The anti-colonial movement united diverse groups of Indians — peasants, workers, industrialists, students — against British rule, creating a shared sense of collective identity and belonging. Movements like the Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience Movements brought together different classes and communities in a common struggle, fostering nationalism through a shared goal of independence and shared symbols (like the national flag and Bharat Mata) that unified people beyond regional or religious identities.
keyPoints: The anti-colonial struggle united diverse social groups against a common ruler.
Mass movements (Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience) brought different classes/communities together.
Shared symbols (flag, Bharat Mata) helped unify people beyond regional/religious identity.

text: OR: Why did Gandhiji say 'Satyagraha is pure soul-force'? Explain by giving two arguments. (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: (1) Satyagraha relied on the power of truth and moral conviction, not physical force or violence, to fight injustice — even someone without physical strength could participate by holding firmly to truth and non-violence. (2) It aimed to invite the oppressor to change their viewpoint through moral persuasion rather than coercion, meaning even the poorest and weakest could take part in this struggle through nonviolent civil disobedience.
keyPoints: Argument 1: Satyagraha relies on truth and moral conviction, not physical force.
Argument 2: it persuades the oppressor morally rather than coercing them by violence.
Note that this let even the physically weak or poor participate in the struggle.

text: Explain any two problems of the 'global ecology' arising due to indiscriminate use of resources. (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: (1) Deforestation and loss of biodiversity from over-exploiting forest resources for timber, agriculture and industry. (2) Global warming and climate change from excessive burning of fossil fuels and greenhouse gas emissions, along with depletion of the ozone layer, threatening ecological balance worldwide.
keyPoints: Problem 1: deforestation and biodiversity loss from resource over-exploitation.
Problem 2: global warming/climate change from excessive fossil fuel use.
Both problems should be tied to 'indiscriminate' (unregulated, excessive) resource use.

text: Suggest any two measures to remove gender inequality. (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: (1) Ensure equal access to education and equal pay/opportunities for women in the workforce so they are not economically disadvantaged. (2) Encourage greater political participation and representation of women (e.g. reservation of seats in local bodies) and strictly enforce laws against gender-based discrimination and violence.
keyPoints: Measure 1: equal access to education and equal pay/opportunity at work.
Measure 2: greater political representation (e.g. reserved seats) and strict enforcement of anti-discrimination laws.
Both measures should target structural, not just attitudinal, change.

text: How did the process of liberalisation initiated in India in the 1990s promote globalisation? Explain. (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: Liberalisation removed trade barriers and restrictions (tariffs, licensing requirements) that the government had earlier imposed on business and investment, letting foreign companies invest and operate more freely in India and Indian companies compete internationally. This easier flow of imports/exports, foreign investment, and collaboration with MNCs is what integrated India more closely into the world market, promoting globalisation.
keyPoints: Liberalisation removed trade barriers/restrictions like tariffs and licensing.
This let foreign companies invest more freely and Indian firms compete internationally.
Easier trade/investment flows integrated India into the world market, promoting globalisation.

text: 'Tribal peasants interpreted the message of Mahatma Gandhi and the idea of Swaraj in yet another way.' Explain the statement in the context of the Non-Cooperation Movement. (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: Tribal peasants (e.g. in the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh, led by Alluri Sitaram Raju) did not understand Swaraj simply as constitutional self-government; they interpreted Gandhi's message in their own way, believing his power could help restore their traditional rights to forest resources and that Swaraj meant liberation from oppressive forest laws. This sometimes led to militant action (like Raju's guerrilla movement) rather than strictly non-violent methods, showing how tribals adapted the nationalist message to their own local grievances.
keyPoints: Tribal peasants linked Swaraj to restoring their own rights over forest resources, not just self-government.
Give the example of Alluri Sitaram Raju's movement in the Gudem Hills.
Note that this sometimes took a militant form, differing from Gandhi's own non-violent methods.

text: Read the story of a girl whose family clears, slashes and burns a patch of land for cultivation, irrigating it with water from a bamboo canal, without knowing the fertility will soon decline and they will need to move to a fresh patch. What type of farming is this family doing? Describe any two of its characteristics. (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: This is Primitive Subsistence Farming (also called slash-and-burn or shifting cultivation, 'Jhum' in North-East India). (1) It depends on monsoon rains, natural soil fertility and suitable environmental conditions, using traditional tools like the hoe and dao rather than modern inputs. (2) A patch of land is cleared and cultivated for a few years until soil fertility declines, after which the plot is abandoned and the farmer moves to a new patch, letting the old land recover naturally.
keyPoints: Identify the farming type: Primitive Subsistence/shifting ('Jhum') cultivation.
Characteristic 1: dependent on monsoon and natural soil fertility, using traditional tools.
Characteristic 2: land is abandoned and a new patch cleared once fertility declines.

text: 'That democratic system of government is considered good in which maximum number of citizens are made stakeholders in political power.' Explain the statement with suitable arguments. (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: A democracy is considered better when political power and its benefits are shared as widely as possible, since democracy is fundamentally the rule of the people. (1) Wide participation makes government accountable to a larger section of society rather than a small elite, preventing power from concentrating in a few hands. (2) When more citizens have a stake in political power, it strengthens the system's legitimacy and public trust, reducing alienation and social conflict since more groups feel included in governance.
keyPoints: Explain that democracy means rule of the people, so wider power-sharing fits its core idea.
Argument 1: wide participation increases accountability and prevents power concentrating in a few hands.
Argument 2: broader stakes in power build legitimacy, trust, and reduce social alienation/conflict.

text: Explain the importance of political parties in democracy. (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: Political parties are important because they contest elections and give voters a choice of candidates/policies; they form and run the government, translating the popular mandate into policy; they act as a link between people and government, aggregating and voicing diverse public demands; and the opposition parties keep the ruling party in check, ensuring accountability. Without parties, elections and governance would lack organisation, and public participation would be far more fragmented.
keyPoints: Parties give voters organised choices of candidates and policies.
The winning party forms government; others act as opposition, ensuring accountability.
Parties link people to government, organising and voicing public demands.

text: OR: Why did India adopt the multiparty system? Explain with suitable arguments. (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: India's vast social diversity (of region, language, religion, caste) meant no single party could represent every group's interests, so a multiparty system emerged, giving space to both smaller/regional parties and national parties to represent varied interests. This also allows coalition governments reflecting a broader base of opinion, rather than concentrating representation in just one or two parties, as a two-party system would.
keyPoints: India's vast social diversity cannot be represented by one or two parties alone.
A multiparty system lets regional and national parties represent varied interests.
It allows coalition governments reflecting a broader base of opinion than a two-party system.

text: Explain the difference between public and private sector of Indian economy with example. (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: The public sector is owned and operated by the government (e.g. Indian Railways, ONGC), typically aiming at public welfare alongside profit, often providing essential services or infrastructure. The private sector is owned and operated by private individuals or companies (e.g. Tata Motors, Reliance Industries), primarily driven by profit motive, operating in competitive markets across various industries.
keyPoints: Public sector: government-owned, aims at welfare alongside profit (e.g. Indian Railways).
Private sector: privately owned, profit-driven (e.g. Tata Motors, Reliance).
Give at least one concrete example for each sector.
